text.p: The following are the main stories from Wednesday morning's German newspapers:
FRANKFURTER ALLGEMEINE ZEITUNG
- Six economic institues predict further recovery in 1997 but caution picture in eastern Germany is less rosy.
- Justice ministry plans tougher penalties for illegal disposal of toxic waste.
- Court rules state of Lower Saxony must pay compensation to federal government for delaying construction of nuclear waste depot.
- Six institutes call for wages to be linked more closely to productivity.
HANDELSBLATT
- Finance Minister Theo Waigel pledges Germany will meet Maastricht criteria for European economic and monetary union (EMU).
- German Trade Union Federation (DGB) says Federal Labour Office needs government subsidy of six billion marks for next year.
- Deutsche Bank targets investment banking market in Asia.
- Demand weak in mechanical engineering sector.
- Growth in advertising sector less rapid this year than last, trade association says.
SUEDDEUTSCHE ZEITUNG
- Six institutes criticise policies of Finance Minister Theo Waigel.
- Bavaria says it will introduce questionnaire for public sector employees quizzing them about possibe links to Church of Scientology.
- Party managers battle to track down members of parliament for emergency debate on government finance policy.
- Court rules state telecommunications company Deutsche Telekom does not have exclusive copyright on information in telephone directories.
DIE WELT
- Research Minister Juergen Ruettgers interrupts Asia trip to fly back to Bonn for debate on government finance policy.
- HBV retail workers' trade union warns longer shop opening hours mean service in stores will deteriorate.
- ZDH building trades' association criticises employers for not daring to cut workers' sick pay.
